Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Define and describe the epidemiology of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
Review the pathogenesis and natural history of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
Determine the appropriate clinical and radiographic evaluation for patients with adolescent
idiopathic scoliosis.
Define treatment objectives and surgical techniques for patients with adolescent idiopathic
scoliosis.
Definition
Three-dimensional spinal deformity in children aged 10 to 18 years1,2


Definition
Idiopathic scoliosis is a diagnosis of exclusion that is made after all other causes of the
disorder have been ruled out. The scoliotic spine deviates from the midline in the
coronal plane, typically has decreased thoracic kyphosis, and rotates maximally at the
apex of the curve in the axial plane. The rotational deformity results in prominence of
the chest wall and the lumbar musculature. In adolescents, the most progressive
idiopathic thoracic scoliosis is convex to the right side of the chest.
Epidemiology of Idiopathic Scoliosis
Prevalence—Small to moderate curves are more common and occur in males and females
equally, whereas more severe curves are rare and are much more prevalent in females.
The incidence of curves between 10° to 20° is 3%.
The incidence of curves greater than 30° is 0.3%.
The female-to-male ratio for curves greater than 30° is 10:1.
The female-to-male ratio for smaller curves is 1:1.
Pathogenesis of Idiopathic Scoliosis
Connective tissue abnormalities
Bone or collagen abnormalities are thought to result in misshapen vertebrae or osteopenia,
resulting in structural collapse of the spine.
Muscular disorders are thought to result in spinal imbalance and deformity progression.
Genetic theories3
Vertebral growth abnormalities4,5

Pathogenesis of Idiopathic Scoliosis
A clear increased incidence of scoliosis in family members of affected individuals
suggests a genetic component to the disease; however, the exact genes involved in
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001177
2/25

adolescent idiopathic scoliosis remain unknown. Environmental factors, especially
pubertal hormones, may influence disease course and progression.
Asymmetric growth between the right and left sides of the spine or relative overgrowth
of the anterior spinal column is thought to be associated with deformity progression. As
the asymmetry worsens, the spine may buckle by rotating laterally to maintain global
balance.
Natural History of Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
6,7
Increased incidence of pain in adults if progressive deformity is unmanaged
Curves greater than 90° are associated with cardiopulmonary dysfunction, early death, pain,
and decreased self-image.
Pulmonary function becomes limited as thoracic scoliosis increases beyond 70°.
The social effect of scoliosis varies, depending on the individual and societal expectations.
Some studies have reported decreased marriage rates in affected individuals, and other
studies have reported increased rates of psychosocial impairment.
Curve progression
Magnitude of deformity at presentation
Skeletal maturity
Continued progression if curve is greater than 45° before skeletal maturity
After skeletal maturity
Thoracic curves greater than 50° will progress 1° to 2° per year.
Lumbar curves greater than 40° will progress 1° to 2° per year.

Natural History of Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
If treatment options are considered in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis, the long-
term effects of the disease should be appreciated. Although the risk of curve progression
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001177
3/25

is strongly associated with peak height velocity (PHV), certain curves will continue to
progress even after skeletal maturity.
Genetics of Idiopathic Scoliosis
Idiopathic scoliosis is a complex disease with a polygenic background.
Exome sequencing has shown that, similar to Marfan syndrome, variants of fibrillin 1 and 2
genes are associated with idiopathic scoliosis.
Individual genotyping also has revealed a highly important association with the fibrillar
collagen (COL11A2) gene.
Genome-wide association studies have found variations in the ladybird homeobox-1 (LBX1)
gene, the G protein?coupled receptor-126 (GPR126) gene, and a locus distal to the paired box-1
(PAX1) transcription factor that have all been confirmed in zebrafish.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Clinical Presentation
Physical examination
The back and trunk are inspected for asymmetry of shoulder heights, scapular position, waist
asymmetry, and leg-length discrepancy. Coronal balance may be identified by evaluating
trunk position relative to waist position and the distance from a C7 plumb line to the central
sacral vertical line.
Skin should be inspected for birthmarks, such as café-au-lait spots/axillary freckles
(concerning for neurofibromatosis type 1) or evidence of spinal dysraphism with a sacral
dimple or hairy patch.
The Adams forward bend test may identify rotational deformity in the upper thoracic, main
thoracic, and thoracolumbar regions. Typically, an angle of trunk rotation of 5° to 7° is
associated with a coronal Cobb angle of 15° to 20°. Occasionally, the angle of trunk rotation
and curve magnitude do not correlate (Figure 1).
A thorough neurologic examination should be performed to assess motor and sensory
function in the upper and lower extremities. Gait, toe, and heel walking, as well as squat and
single-leg stance should be assessed. Deep tendon reflexes and abdominal reflexes should
be evaluated.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001177
4/25

Leg-length discrepancy is assessed by evaluating the top of the bilateral iliac crests. Angle of
trunk rotation measurements should be obtained with a shoe lift to level the pelvis in
patients with a notable discrepancy.
Figure 1 Posterior view clinical photograph of a patient with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis shows
the Adams forward bend test. Note the rotational trunk deformity indicated by the asymmetry of
the ribs, with the right rib cage being more prominent than the left rib cage. (Reproduced from
Oetgen ME, Martin BD: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, in Martus JE, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge
Update: Pediatrics, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp
351-363.)
Radiography
Positioning
Assessment of the deformity
Sagittal spinopelvic parameters—Pelvic incidence, sacral slope, and pelvic tilt can be
measured on lateral radiographs. The spinopelvic parameters are important to define a
patient’s normal sagittal profile.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001177
5/25

Coronal and sagittal balance can be assessed using the C7 plumb line on PA and lateral
radiographs (Figure 2).
The preoperative flexibility of spinal deformities can be assessed with bending radiographs
(with the patient upright or supine over a bolster).
Figure 2 Full-length PA (A) and lateral (B) drawings of the spine demonstrate how to measure the
common Cobb angles, the C7 plumb line, and the center sacral vertical line (CSVL). The CSVL
helps identify the stable of best bisected vertebra or disk at the thoracolumbar junction. On the
lateral drawing, a vertical line from the posterior superior corner of S1 helps identify the stable
sagittal vertebra (SSV). Spinopelvic measurements of sacral slope, pelvic tilt, and pelvic incidence
also are shown. (Reproduced with permission from Rady Children’s Hospital, San Diego, CA.)
Computed tomography
CT is rarely indicated in patients with idiopathic scoliosis; however, it may be used to assess
vertebral abnormalities, evaluate pedicle morphology, or rule out spondylolysis or other
pathologies.
Magnetic resonance imaging
Most adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis do not require MRI (exceptions follow), which often
is used to evaluate intraspinal pathology, including Chiari malformation, syrinx, or spinal
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001177
6/25

tether.
Indications: left thoracic curve, short angular curve, thoracic kyphosis, rapidly progressive
deformity, neurologic findings, or pain
Assessments of skeletal maturity
For PHV—Mean PHV in adolescence is 8 to 10 cm per year, with approximately one-half of
this growth from the spine. A number of variables can predict a child’s progression along his
or her growth curve.
Association with menarche—Generally, onset of menses occurs approximately 12 months
after the most rapid stage of skeletal growth.
Risser grade8
Sanders stage

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Assessment of ossification of the left iliac apophysis ranges from grade 0 (no ossification)
to grade 5 (fully ossified). Risser grade 0 encompasses a wide age range in skeletally
immature patients, and grade 1 typically occurs after PHV.
The patient history should document the manner in which the deformity was first
identified (eg, well-child check, school screening, parental observation) and whether
other family members are affected. Physical changes associated with growth or puberty
should be assessed. Understanding a patient’s developmental milestones may reveal
other etiologies for scoliosis. In addition, the presence or absence of back pain and red
flag symptoms, such as night pain, weakness, sensory changes, balance or gait
disturbance, and bowel or bladder function, are important.
Upright PA and lateral radiographs of the spine are used to assess spinal deformity. The
arm position should be standardized, with the shoulders in neutral, the elbows flexed,
and the hands at chest level. Alternatively, hands may be placed above the level of the
shoulders for simultaneous evaluation of Sanders staging of the hand and determination
of growth remaining.9 Techniques that minimize radiation exposure in sensitive tissues,
such as the breasts, thyroid, and ovaries, should be used.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001177
7/25

The Cobb method quantifies the magnitude of spinal deformity in the upper thoracic,
main thoracic, and thoracolumbar regions of the spine in the coronal plane and the
magnitude of thoracic kyphosis and lumbar lordosis in the sagittal plane. Interobserver
and intraobserver variations in Cobb measurements are thought to be approximately 5°.
Vertebral rotation can be estimated by evaluating the asymmetry of the pedicles and
spinous process or quantified using the methods described by Perdriolle and Vidal10 or
Lam et al.11
Assessment of ossification of the physes in the metacarpals and phalanges ranges from
stage 1 (digital epiphyses not covered) to stage 8 (all phalangeal physes and distal radial
physis completely closed). Stage 3 (most digits are capped) correlates with PHV and early
rapid adolescent growth spurt.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Bracing
Bracing indications12
Scoliosis Research Society criteria: 25° to 45° curve, Risser grade 0 to 2, Sanders stage 4 or
less
Bracing outcomes13
Schroth method

Bracing
Several types of braces have been developed for the management of adolescent
idiopathic scoliosis. The Boston underarm thoracolumbosacral orthosis is most often
used. The Charleston and Providence nighttime bending braces offer alternatives for
managing flexible spine deformities. Rigo-Cheneau braces, which use axial plane
derotational forces, also have gained popularity; however, fewer high-quality data
support their use compared with other methods.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001177
8/25

Adherence with brace use is a main factor in treatment success. A recent randomized
clinical trial that used a temperature monitor to document brace adherence
demonstrated that 72% of brace wearers avoided surgical treatment compared with 48%
of patients in the observational group. More than 90% of the patients who wore the
brace for 13 hours or more avoided surgical treatment.
To avoid surgical stabilization, scoliosis-specific exercises designed to derotate, elongate,
and stabilize the spine are good adjuncts to brace management.
Surgical Management
Goals of surgical management are to prevent curve progression, attain three-dimensional
deformity correction, and achieve long-lasting correction.
Indications for surgical management are based on curve magnitude, clinical deformity, risk of
progression, and curve pattern.14
In skeletally immature patients, thoracic curves greater than 45° to 50° should be corrected.
Curves greater than 50° with documented progression despite skeletal maturity also should
be corrected.
Thoracolumbar curves smaller than 40° may cause considerable clinical deformity and may
be corrected in skeletally immature patients.
Classifications for surgical management
King-Moe classification15
Lenke classification16,17
Neurophysiologic monitoring
Allows for real-time assessment of neural structures intraoperatively
A systematic approach to intraoperative neuromonitoring changes should be used to gain
control of the operating room, address anesthetic and systemic factors (eg, blood pressure,
temperature), address technical issues with neuromonitoring, and determine the surgical
steps that may have caused intraoperative neuromonitoring changes.
Selection of fusion levels18,19
Vertebral definitions (Figure 3)
End vertebrae: most tilted vertebrae from horizontal in the coronal plane defining the top
and bottom of each curve

Stable vertebra: vertebra most closely bisected by the central sacral vertical line
Neutral vertebra: least rotated vertebra in the axial plane based on symmetric pedicles and
midline spinous process
Thoracic major curves
Upper instrumented vertebra (UIV): based on shoulder balance
High left shoulder: UIV = T2
Balanced shoulder: UIV = T3
High right shoulder: UIV = T4
Lowest instrumented vertebra (LIV): based on lumbar curve modifier20,21 (Figure 4)
AL lumbar modifier: LIV = 1- stable vertebra
AR lumbar modifier: LIV = last substantially touched vertebra
B lumbar modifier: LIV = stable vertebra
C lumbar modifier: LIV = 1+ stable vertebrae
To avoid distal junctional kyphosis, evaluate the sagittal stable vertebra and ensure that the
LIV is anterior to the posterior sacral line or that the instrumented fusion does not end in a
region of kyphosis at the thoracolumbar junction.22
Main thoracolumbar curves
UIV = upper end vertebra
LIV = L3 if the L3/L4 disk is open to the right or parallel (Figure 5)
LIV = L4 if the L3/L4 disk is open to the left
LIV = L3 if the center of L3 is less than 3.5 cm from the central sacral vertebral line23

Anterior techniques24
Anterior instrumentation and fusion of the thoracic spine was popular in the 1990s and early
2000s.25-27
Anterior release (thoracoscopic versus open) may be used in patients with a large curve
(>90°), young patients (open triradiate cartilage), and patients with a stiff curve (<35°
flexibility).28-30
Anterior non-fusion treatment options (vertebral body tethering)
Gaining popularity; however, indications continue to be refined and longer-term outcomes
are required (Video 1)
Posterior correction techniques31-33

Surgical complications34,35
Blood loss requiring transfusion (<5%)
Gastrointestinal complications
Superior mesenteric artery syndrome; rare complication occurring in less than 1% of
patients
Pulmonary complications (approximately 1%)
Neurologic deficits (0.3% to 1.4%)
Implant failure/pseudarthrosis
Surgical site infection (1% to 2%)


Surgical Management
This traditional classification system uses coronal radiographs to determine whether to
manage a thoracic curve and whether to manage thoracic and lumbar curves.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:10 AM
AAOS | Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001177
15/25

Limitations of this classification system include lack of sagittal plane analysis and
interobserver reliability issues.
This comprehensive classification system was primarily designed to define structural and
nonstructural curves and guide surgical treatment decisions for all curve types. It
considers coronal and sagittal deformities and curve flexibility on bending radiographs.
Lenke type 1 through type 4 curves are major thoracic curves (ie, the thoracic curve is
greater in magnitude than the thoracolumbar curve). Lenke type 5 and type 6 curves
define major thoracolumbar or lumbar curves. The lumbar modifier categorizes the
magnitude of coronal lumbar deformity in relation to the central sacral vertical line.
Sagittal plane assessments are performed to evaluate regions of kyphosis in the upper
thoracic, main thoracic, and thoracolumbar junctions and to determine the need for
extension of instrumented fusion. Structural curves have substantial kyphosis or do not
bend to less than 25° in the coronal plane. The Lenke classification recommends surgical
instrumentation and fusion of all structural regions of a spinal deformity (Figure 6).
Transcranial motor-evoked potentials apply a train of high-voltage stimuli to electrodes
on the surface of the head to activate motor pathways and produce muscle contraction.
Bite blocks are used to avoid injury to the tongue or teeth. In addition, clinicians should
be aware that the procedure may trigger seizures in susceptible patients.
Upper and lower extremity somatosensory-evoked potentials also are used to monitor
spinal cord function intraoperatively. Peripheral nerves are stimulated (ie, the median
nerve near the wrist or the posterior tibial nerve at the ankle), and the impulses are
carried back up the spine through the dorsal columns to the sensory cortex. Injuries to
the dorsal column pathways are typical, with a more than 50% decrease in amplitude or
a 10% increase in latency of baseline potentials. Transcranial motor-evoked potential
signals are more sensitive and quicker to respond to spinal cord activity changes than
somatosensory-evoked potential signals.
Spontaneous electromyographic activity is recorded in various muscle groups
throughout a surgical procedure. Compression or stretch of a nerve and hypothermia or
ischemia causes depolarization of the axons, resulting in spontaneous action potentials,
which are recorded by the electrodes placed in the muscles. Triggered electromyography

9/3/26, 7:10 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001177
16/25

is used to verify proper screw placement. Each pedicle screw is stimulated, and the
threshold required to record electromyographic activity because of adjacent nerve root
stimulation is determined. Screws with a stimulation threshold less than or equal to 5
mA are most often misplaced, and screws with a stimulation threshold greater than 10
mA generally are thought to be well placed.
Posterior instrumented fusion currently is the preferred treatment option for the
management of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (Figure 7). Meticulous subperiosteal
dissection of the posterior elements of the spine is performed. Facetectomy mobilizes
the spinal deformity, allowing for fusion mass. Ponte-type posterior column releases
may improve spinal mobility and sagittal and axial plane correction (Figure 8). Segmental
instrumentation typically involves the use of pedicle screws or hybrid constructs.
Figure 7 Images of the spine of a patient with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis show
posterior instrumented fusion. A, Preoperative full-length PA radiograph demonstrates a
Lenke type 1AL curve (L4 tilt to the left). B, Intraoperative photograph shows posterior
spine exposure. C, Intraoperative photograph shows the use of an ultrasonic bone
scalpel to perform facetectomies. D, Intraoperative photograph shows the placement of
uniplanar pedicle screws segmentally via a freehand technique. E, Postoperative full-
length PA radiograph demonstrates posterior instrumented fusion from T5 through T12.

The lowest instrumented vertebra is one proximal to stable. High-density fixation was
used on the concavity of the deformity, and low-density fixation was used on the
convexity of the deformity. (Reproduced with permission from Newton PO, Upasani VV:
Posterior spinal fusion for idiopathic scoliosis, in Wiesel SW, ed: Operative Techniques in
Orthopaedic Surgery, ed 2. Philadelphia, PA, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2015, vol 2, pp
1778-1785.)
Figure 8 Intraoperative photograph of a spine shows Ponte-type osteotomies with
excision of the spinous process, intraspinous ligaments, superior articulating facet,
capsule, and ligamentum flavum. (Reproduced with permission from Newton PO,
Upasani VV: Posterior spinal fusion for idiopathic scoliosis, in Wiesel SW, ed: Operative
Techniques in Orthopaedic Surgery, ed 2. Philadelphia, PA, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins,
2015, vol 2, pp 1778-1785.)
Spinal deformity correction may involve a number of techniques, including differential
rod contouring with a rod-derotation maneuver, in situ rod contouring, compression-
distraction, and en bloc versus segmental spinal derotation (Figures 9, 10, and 11).
Surgical management of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis deformity has become much
safer in the past few decades. The remarkable corrective power of new instrumentation
methods in combination with improved surgical skills, spinal cord monitoring, methods
to minimize blood loss, and advances in anesthesia have decreased complication rates.
